question: Does a class-free, feature-engineered gradient-boosting Q-function match or beat a classical MLP Q-network on multi-resource allocation as the number of items grows?
method: Synthetic multi-dimensional knapsack MDP solved sequentially; fitted Q-iteration with a fixed transition budget; both Q-functions trained on identical transitions; evaluated by greedy rollout on held-out instances against a greedy+local-search reference.

dataset.name: Seeded synthetic multi-dimensional knapsack instances (numpy generator)
dataset.source_url: numpy synthetic generator (no download); models: https://scikit-learn.org, https://lightgbm.readthedocs.io

metric_name: mean achieved value / greedy+local-search reference value on test instances
baseline: sklearn MLPRegressor (64,64) on standardised raw state-action features; classical Rainbow-DQN stand-in without distributional, dueling or quantum parts.
improved: LightGBM regressor Q-function on engineered features (value-to-resource ratios, slack ratios, tightness, value and density ranks, feasible-item fraction, remaining capacity, item rank), same transitions and budget.
notes: Synthetic instances, not the paper's data; the paper's quantum model is not reproduced. Hyper-parameters are fixed a priori and nothing was tuned on the test set. Feasibility is enforced by action masking, so feasibility rate is a sanity check. Reference is a heuristic, so ratios can exceed 1. Only 3 seeds and 50 test instances per size: differences are noisy.
